Ralf Schumacher says Oscar Piastri is McLaren's second driver after struggles with new regulations. The Australian trails Norris heavily in 2026.

Ralf Schumacher says Oscar Piastri is McLaren's second driver after struggles with new regulations. The Australian trails Norris heavily in 2026.

Het laatste F1 nieuws, resultaten en informatie over Formule 1 en Max Verstappen Oscar Piastri has become McLaren's second driver following a difficult start to the 2026 season, Oscar Piastri has become McLaren's second driver following a difficult start to the 2026 season, according to Ralf Schumacher. The former F1 driver says the Australian, who trails team-mate Lando Norris heavily in the championship, would no longer be considered a team leader candidate by top teams. Schumacher's assessment comes as Norris has won twice in succession while Piastri has managed just two podiums from a season disrupted by mechanical failures and a visible performance gap to his British team-mate.Piastri's campaign began with back-to-back retirements before the race even started, forcing him onto the back foot from the opening weekend. He recovered with consecutive podium finishes but has not returned to the top three since. Norris, by contrast, has multiple wins to his name and is firmly in contention for the world championship. The contrast is stark: Piastri sits seventh with 104 points, while Norris leads the title fight.Schumacher's paddock testSpeaking on the German podcast Backstage Boxengasse, Schumacher framed Piastri's situation in terms of how teams would view him today. "If you go into the paddock now and a team is looking for a leader who can lead the championship, a year ago you would have absolutely wanted Piastri," Schumacher said. "I fear that would no longer be the case today. He is now, for the time being, number two, but the season is still long."Schumacher was careful not to dismiss Piastri's underlying speed. "I have to say, Piastri is incredibly fast and you also need someone who scores points for you," he noted. The German added that Piastri has not suddenly become a poor driver. "He's not making mistakes, he's just slower than Norris at the moment, but that can change depending on the development phase of the car."A fortunate dynamic for McLarenSchumacher suggested McLaren has benefited from the timing of Piastri's slump. "I think it was also a bit of luck that Oscar Piastri, I wouldn't say he's having a hard time, but he is struggling at the moment," he said. The implication is clear: with Norris in title form, McLaren can focus its resources without internal friction. Piastri's role has shifted from championship contender to reliable points scorer, a dynamic that suits the team but diminishes his stock in the wider paddock.The shift marks a reversal of the 2025 season, when Piastri appeared a serious title candidate for much of the year before fading late. Norris ultimately claimed that championship, and the hierarchy within McLaren has calcified this season. Piastri remains seventh in the standings, a position that reflects consistency but not the front-running pace he showed in his early F1 career.Reputation and the development windowSchumacher's warning about being "careful" when judging Piastri reflects the volatility of car development cycles. Regulation changes can expose or flatter driving styles, and McLaren's 2026 package appears better suited to Norris. Whether that persists through upgrades and setup evolution will determine if Piastri can reclaim parity. For now, though, his status as a potential team leader elsewhere has taken a hit. Top teams looking for a number one driver would hesitate, and that hesitation alone is a problem for a driver who, 12 months ago, was considered one of the sport's rising elite.Piastri's challenge is not just performance but perception. He has time to reverse both, but only if McLaren's development arc shifts in his favour. Schumacher's assessment is a reminder that F1 reputations are built and dismantled over short windows, and Piastri is currently in one that counts against him.

Oscar Piastri has recounted the "painful" issues he endured at the Formula 1 2026 Dutch Grand Prix that resulted in a 32-second gap to his McLaren team-mate A clinical victory for Lando Norris left half the McLaren garage ecstatic. However, Piastri had little to celebrate following a sixth-place finish at Zandvoort. The Australian qualified well, starting on the second row, alongside Championship leader Kimi Antonelli. A tumultuous opening lap saw Piastri in fifth, where he would take the red-flag restart. But after overtaking George Russell and Charles Leclerc, it momentarily looked to be McLaren's day. Unfortunately, his race fell apart as the race progressed. A series of unfortunate strategy calls left Piastri falling behind his rivals. An early slow stop saw the 25-year-old lose crucial track position to Russell, and then a second stint on the hard tyres continued to derail his Sunday. Piastri was subject to a 5.4 second pitstop early in the race Following the disappointing drive, Piastri explained that his strategy was pretty clearly wrong compared to his rival's. "The idea was to start on the hards and then go to the end, but it became clear pretty quickly that the hards weren't actually great - but I don't think that side of things was much of an issue," Piastri told media, including Motorsport Week However, he emphasised that the strategy was not the sole factor in his underwhelming result. "Obviously, the slow first stop was a bit painful, and the pace afterwards was painful, and there were a lot of different strategies, but I don't think ours was really the issue of our race." Piastri explains 'tricky' F1 issues during his second stint The degradation on Piastri's opening set of hard tyres was manageable, but his second stint proved far more problematic. After initially feeling comfortable, the Australian quickly lost front-end grip. Unable to match the pace of his rivals around. "The degradation on the first set of hards felt okay. The second set was good for about five laps, and then I completely ran out of front tyres," Piastri explained. "So there is not necessarily one thing that's going wrong, but the stint on that tyre was very tricky." "Starting in fifth [for the restart], I was able to go around the outside, and it was a lot nicer because I picked one space up. And then George's power unit selected reverse down to Turn 7... Then it went pretty downhill from there." Despite briefly making progress and looking capable of challenging towards the front, Piastri admitted there was no single explanation for why his afternoon unravelled. "There's not really one clear issue. I think in the first stint, things felt reasonable; there was a bit of a tough period in the middle, but by the end of the stint, it felt pretty good. Then the second stint on the hards was okay for the first five laps, and then a mess." Piastri acknowledged that McLaren's machinery was not the problem. With his team-mate now securing back-to-back victories with McLaren's current package. "Lando has won the race by quite a lot, so I think the car is in a good place. It's been quick the last two weekends, and I think these two tracks suit the car well; it is just that, for whatever reason, I've not been able to get the pace out of it." The Australian currently sits seventh in the Drivers' Standings, 55 points behind Norris. Piastri will look toward circuits like Monza to capitalise on McLaren's pace and move him closer to his rivals. READ MORE – Lewis Hamilton issues F1 fighting talk with Ferrari social media apology

items.article_search_text: Lando Norris says the fight's back on for the world title after his Dutch Grand Prix win, but... World champ Lando Norris has handed McLaren a third successive Dutch Grand Prix ‌victory at Zandvoort -- but his Australian teammate Oscar Piastri was again back at the drawing board after being a mere also-ran in a race he won last year. There was plenty of drama in a contest that had to be re-started on a damp track on Sunday after home hero Max Verstappen crashed on the opening lap before world champion Norris then went on to make it back-to-back F1 victories with a brilliant drive to pep up his title fightback. But as Norris declared "the fight is still on", there was to be no similar upturn in fortunes for deflated Piastri, who had to settle for sixth as he again couldn't match his teammate's pace. It was after this race in 2025 -- the last time Piastri tasted F1 victory -- that the Melbourne driver looked on top of the world, 34 points clear of the chasing pack and seemingly unstoppable en route to what looked sure to be his first drivers' title. But his late-season slump has since been followed by a calamitous start to the 2026 campaign from which the Australian has never wholly recovered as Norris has proved a step ahead most weekends. "A frustrating afternoon with a disappointing result, but still some points on the board," sighed Piastri, who's pondering if his lack of pace compared to Norris is down to their driving styles. "The first stint felt okay, and then after that I just had nothing," Piastri said, pulling no punches. "I don't know why, but plenty to look into.The first stint felt reasonable, but from the second stint onwards, the pace was simply not there, and it became a real struggle." Piastri did enjoy one brilliant early overtake on the restart to whip past George Russell into third place, but luck still wasn't on his side. "A slow pit-stop after that didn't help, but the fundamental issue was the lack of pace, which is something we'll work on ahead of Monza," he shrugged. Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli finished second to increase his championship lead over teammate George Russell, who obeyed team orders to let the young Italian, on fresher tyres, through late in ‌the race and ‌then held ⁠off Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton for third. Norris, who started on pole but had to fight back after losing the lead to Antonelli at the re-start, followed up his victory in Hungary last month to move to fourth in the championship on 159 points, still an aching 83 points behind Antonelli (242) but only 24 behind Hamilton and Russell (183). But Piastri is out of the picture, in a distant seventh place on 104, behind fifth-placed Charles Leclerc (155) and sixth-placed Verstappen (112), who crashed out of his ‌home Grand Prix at the end of the first ‌lap after his Red Bull went into the concrete wall on the banked corner before skidding back ‌across the track. Though a wheel broke off and ran loose, scattering debris around, Verstappen was able to walk away unscathed, but it was a sad way for the Netherlands' greatest driver to leave the Zandvoort circuit, which will drop off the ⁠F1 calendar next season, in front of his adoring fans. But Norris was ebullient. "Let's keep bringing upgrades. Let's keep bringing performance. The fight is still on. Let's keep going," boomed the 2024 Zandvoort winner. New Zealander Liam Lawson, a stand-in for injured Isack Hadjar, was seventh for Red Bull, Nico Hulkenberg eighth for Audi ​with Fernando Alonso putting Aston Martin, with a more powerful Honda engine, back in the ​points in ninth. With agencies Australian Associated Press
